title: Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact
one_line: A benchmark study probing whether large language models can separate first-person belief, third-person belief, knowledge and fact, finding they systematically fail on false first-person beliefs.
key_claims: Across a large set of true/false statements framed as beliefs, knowledge claims or bare facts, LLMs handled third-person attributions far better than first-person false beliefs.
Models frequently refused to acknowledge that a speaker holds a belief the model judges false, instead correcting the statement rather than attributing the belief.
Models do not consistently apply the factive nature of knowledge (that knowing entails truth), treating knowledge and belief inconsistently across prompts.
Newer/more recent model releases performed better on some conditions but did not eliminate the first-person false-belief gap.
Authors argue these failures matter for high-stakes epistemic settings such as medicine, law and journalism, where distinguishing what someone believes from what is true is essential.
limitations: Findings are benchmark-based on templated statements, which may not reflect behaviour in open-ended conversation.
Results are tied to specific model versions and prompting strategies available at the time of testing.
The benchmark probes surface outputs, not internal representations, so it cannot establish whether models lack an epistemic distinction or merely fail to express it.
Coverage of languages, domains and belief types is limited relative to real-world epistemic discourse.
open_questions: Would fine-tuning or targeted instruction on epistemic attribution close the first-person false-belief gap, or is it architectural?
Do internal probes reveal a belief/knowledge distinction that the output layer fails to surface?
Does the failure degrade performance on downstream tasks such as clinical or legal note interpretation?
